guide.summary: Forgejo documents an OAuth2 Authorization Code grant with PKCE or confidential clients, and the API accepts OAuth bearer tokens. OAuth2 scopes are not implemented, so the token acts with the user's full rights, and third-party apps receive administrative rights. For the read-only repository-name listing, the mapped endpoint is GET /api/v1/repos/search with the private parameter, using page and limit pagination. The read-only restriction must be enforced by the app. Customer instance details and endpoint behavior remain untested.
guide.recommendation: The requested API test is not ready yet. Resolve the access mapping for List repository names visible to the connected person, including pagination. Use “Find missing request” or add official documentation beside that action.

findings.title: Authorization Code grant with PKCE or confidential client is documented
findings.detail: Forgejo supports the Authorization Code grant with PKCE and OpenID Connect extensions. Third-party use requires registering an application in user settings. Confidential and public client types are both supported, and the authorization and token endpoints are documented per instance.
findings.appliesWhen: Customer connects with OAuth on their own Forgejo instance using the instance base URL.

evidence.quote: Supported OAuth2 Grants At the moment, Forgejo only supports the Authorization Code Grant standard with additional support for the following extensions:

OpenID Connect (OIDC) To use the Authorization Code Grant as a third-party application, it is required to register a new application via the “Settings” ( /user/settings/applications ) section. To test
Authorization Endpoint /login/oauth/authorize Access Token Endpoint /login/oauth/access_token

findings.title: OAuth2 scopes are not implemented; token acts as the user
findings.detail: Scopes are not implemented for OAuth2 tokens, and they can be used to execute any actions on behalf of the user. Scoped tokens are a different mechanism and are not OAuth2 scopes.
findings.appliesWhen: Customer authorizes via OAuth on their own instance.

evidence.quote: OAuth2 scopes are not yet implemented.
Note Scopes are not implemented for OAuth2 tokens and they can be used to
execute any actions on behalf of the user, not just Git-related actions.

findings.title: Third-party OAuth applications receive administrative rights
findings.detail: Third-party applications obtaining a token for a user through an OAuth2 application will have administrative rights. Because scopes are not implemented, the requested read-only use does not limit the token boundary.
findings.appliesWhen: Any customer who authorizes the app via OAuth.

evidence.quote: Note Third-party applications obtaining a token for a user via such an application will have administrative rights.
Forgejo can act as an instance-wide OAuth2 provider. To achieve that, OAuth2 applications must be created on the /admin/applications page.

findings.title: OAuth access tokens are accepted by the API as bearer tokens
findings.detail: Access tokens from Forgejo's OAuth2 provider are accepted via the Authorization Bearer header or token/access_token query parameters. The token is used against the instance base URL.
findings.appliesWhen: Customer connects the app to their own instance.

evidence.quote: OAuth2 Provider Access tokens obtained from Forgejo’s OAuth2 provider are accepted by these methods:
Authorization: Bearer ... header in HTTP headers

steps.title: Register the OAuth2 application on the customer's Forgejo instance
steps.detail: Customer (or admin of their instance) registers an OAuth2 application under user settings at <INSTANCE_BASE_URL>/user/settings/applications, choosing confidential or public client type with the redirect URI for the app. Note the client ID and secret. This is preparation only; no token is requested yet.
steps.doneWhen: Client ID and redirect URI are recorded for the app configuration; the registration page confirms the application exists.

evidence.quote: OpenID Connect (OIDC) To use the Authorization Code Grant as a third-party application, it is required to register a new application via the “Settings” ( /user/settings/applications ) section. To test
Client types Forgejo supports both confidential and public client types, as defined by RFC 6749 .

It is possible for any user to manually register a new OAuth2 application on the /user/settings/applications page for the purpose of using Git credential helpers different from the pre-registered ones.

fields: Client ID and secret: from the customer's registration on their instance

steps.title: Send the user to the consent page and verify the callback
steps.detail: Redirect the connected person to the authorization endpoint with client_id, redirect_uri, response_type=code and a state value. The user consents and is redirected back with code and state; the app must check state matches before continuing. Use PKCE (code_challenge and code_challenge_method) if the app is a public client.
steps.doneWhen: Callback arrives with code and matching state; no code is exchanged yet.

evidence.quote: https://[ YOUR-FORGEJO-URL ]/login/oauth/authorize?client_id=CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=REDIRECT_URI&response_type=code&state=STATE The CLIENT_ID can be obtained by registering an application in the settings. The STATE is a random string that will be
sent back to your application after the user authorizes. The state parameter is optional but should be used to prevent CSRF attacks.
The user will now be asked to authorize your application. If they authorize it, the user will be redirected to the REDIRECT_URL , for example:

fields: redirect_uri: must match the registered URI exactly
state: random value generated by the app
INSTANCE_BASE_URL: your full HTTPS instance URL, without a trailing slash

steps.title: Exchange the authorization code for an access token
steps.detail: POST the code to the documented token endpoint with grant_type=authorization_code, client_id, client_secret (confidential) and the same redirect_uri. For public clients send code_verifier instead of client_secret. The response returns access_token and refresh_token; this is an unexecuted example until a real code is obtained.
steps.doneWhen: Response contains access_token, token_type bearer and expires_in.

steps.title: List visible repository names (first page)
steps.detail: Call the repository search endpoint with private=true and page/limit to read repositories visible to the connected person. Read the repository name from each item's name property in the response body. Pagination uses the Link header and x-total-count. Read-only: this request uses GET only. The token carries full user rights, so the app must enforce read-only behavior itself.
steps.doneWhen: Response is HTTP 200 with a JSON array of repository objects; each name is read from the name property; the Link header and x-total-count are recorded. Boundary check: inspect the actual grant against the documented access above; confirm the outgoing request log contains only the requested operations and no prohibited actions.

steps.title: Request the next page of visible repository names
steps.detail: Repeat the same GET request with the next page number. Continue while the Link header contains rel="next". Stop when no next link is returned or when the page count reaches x-total-count. One or two pages is not a full listing.
steps.doneWhen: All pages are read until no rel="next" link remains and the total matches x-total-count. Boundary check: inspect the actual grant against the documented access above; confirm the outgoing request log contains only the requested operations and no prohibited actions.

evidence.quote: Pagination The API supports pagination. The page and limit parameters are used to specify the page number and the number of items per page. As well, the Link header is
returned with the next, previous, and last page links if there are more than one page. The x-total-count is also returned to indicate the total number of items.
